Both surface and upper-level weather patterns, minus some minor 
tweaks on occasion, are forecast to remain rather static over the 
upcoming weekend and into next week. The only major alteration that 
we will be keeping a close eye on is the potential intrusion of 
Saharan dust that could have some implications on our daily PoPs 
should it come to fruition, but this will be discussed in further 
detailed promptly. High pressure, for a start, will be a frequently 
messaged term and repeatedly relayed over the next several days. In 
the upper levels, a primary ridge axis centered over the subtropical 
Atlantic this weekend will be displaced eastward. Our focus will 
subsequently shift to a new centralized area of high pressure that 
will be taking shape over the northeastern Gulf and later advance 
towards the Southeast/Mid-Atlantic United States where it is 
forecast to amplify quite notably during the upcoming work week. 
ECMWF ensemble data suggests that 500-mb height anomalies could be 
at the 99th percentile for climatology during the second half of the 
weekend and into early next week across our peninsular waters when 
the ridge will be in its earliest fortification phases and closest 
vicinity to South Florida. As the aforementioned shift toward the 
SE/Mid-Atlantic US occurs thereafter, the ridge will only continue 
to strengthen with the ECMWF grand ensemble hinting at mean 500-mb 
heights being at or near all-time records and enveloping maximum 
climatological percentiles through midweek.

As for the implications this will have on South Florida, it will 
help maintain a steady flow aloft primarily out of the east through 
the weekend and into the following work week that will strictly 
refrain us from being impacted from any frontal systems dropping 
south from the higher latitudes but rather by occasional shortwave 
impulses (which won't be of much concern anyways) propagating from 
east to west along the southern periphery of this abnormally 
compelling anticyclonic feature. As mentioned in the beginning of 
this discussion, there are signals amongst the models that a large 
plume of Saharan dust will be riding our low-level easterlies from 
the Greater Antilles through the Bahamas and potentially intruding 
into South Florida late this weekend and into next week, but mainly 
next week. Persistent subtropical ridging will be rambling back and 
forth over the corresponding Atlantic waters through this entire 
long-term period, helping to induce a resolute east to southeasterly 
flow across South Florida this weekend and backing to more of a east 
to northeasterly direction next week. Though long range model data 
and NASA Dust Extinction Aerosol forecast products do show some 
Saharan dust entering our atmospheric column next week, it appears 
as if the forecast has remained consistent for the time being in 
keeping the deepest concentrations to our south over the western 
Caribbean Sea. National Blend of Models (NBM) reflects this, with 
PWATs mostly remaining above 2" through the weekend (60-80th 
percentiles as per climatology) but then dropping sharply come next 
week with these same values being reduced to the 1.7-2.0" range. 
This is also visualized in forecast soundings with drier air and 
larger dew point depressions progressively becoming more evident 
through Wednesday of next week.

With moisture content remaining above average through the weekend 
and our predominant easterly surface flow in place, expect a fairly 
typical summertime pattern to stay firm with showers and 
thunderstorms developing over our local waters during each overnight 
period at the expense of plentiful available instability (CAPE of 
2000-3500 J/Kg as indicated by deterministic models) and the marine 
diurnal max (DMAX) cycle occurring over and around the warm, 
adjacent Gulf Stream waters. Expect these showers and storms to 
gradually push onshore every morning and increase in coverage 
thereafter as they go on to favor our downwind locations i.e. the 
western half of South Florida during the afternoon and early evening 
hours. Localized flooding will be a point of emphasis in and around 
the Naples metro each afternoon this weekend and into early next 
week amid fairly weak flow aloft (bulk shear mainly below 10 kts) 
and the impending Gulf sea breeze counteracting our easterly surface 
flow. It is not until the latter half of this long term forecast 
(specifically Tuesday and Wednesday) that not only our background 
flow starts to strengthen to a degree with the coinciding ridge 
amplification across the SE/Mid-Atlantic US but also an increasing 
easterly flow at the surface looks to offset the Gulf sea breeze 
from pushing inland and thereby minimize the potential for slow-
moving storms/urban flooding. Both storm coverage and intensity are 
still question marks going into next week, as the uncertainty
